title: The Right Word
theme: Precision and nuance: choosing among close words
objectives: I can choose the most exact word to describe how strong, how clear, or how long something is.
I can place faint, mild, moderate, and intense on a scale of strength.
I can revise a vague or wordy sentence so that it is specific and concise.
I can use at least four words from this unit to improve a short piece of my own writing.
rationale: The year ends on the skill that every earlier unit has been building: choosing the most exact word. The ten words come in three kinds of pairs and ladders. Four describe strength of a quality (faint, mild, moderate, intense), two describe precision (vague, specific), two describe length (concise, verbose), and two describe a style of work or speech (thorough, blunt). Students practice placing words on a ladder, replacing vague words with specific ones, and cutting wordy sentences, which are the same moves they will use to revise any piece of writing in grade 7.

words.def: Not clear or exact; hard to understand because details are missing.
words.ex: The directions were so vague that we drove past the turn twice.
words.ex2: She gave a vague answer, saying only that she had been somewhere downtown.
words.nonExample: A note that says 'Meet me at the north gate at 3:15' is not vague.

apps.academic: A vague claim, such as 'it was good,' needs an example to become convincing.
apps.spoken: I have only a vague memory of that day.
apps.writing: Replace a vague word, such as nice or things, with a word that names the exact detail.

cloze.s: When the detective asked where he had been, the suspect gave a ___ answer with no times or places.

cloze2.s: Her ___ memory of the trip was only a blur of buses and snow.

misuse.s: The recipe was vague, giving exact amounts and times for every single step.
misuse.why: Vague means missing exact details; exact amounts and times are specific.

visual.alt: A foggy scene with a question mark.

words.frame: A vague sentence like ___ could be more specific by ___.

words.def: Clear and exact, giving the particular details.
words.ex: Instead of saying 'a long time ago,' give a specific date.
words.ex2: The teacher asked for specific examples from the text to support each claim.
words.nonExample: 'Somewhere around here' is not a specific place.

apps.academic: A specific detail from a text is stronger evidence than a general statement.
apps.spoken: Can you be more specific about when it happened?
apps.writing: Use a specific noun and verb, such as sprinted instead of went, to sharpen a sentence.

cloze.s: To help the repair crew, Mina described the ___ problem: the third window on the left would not close.

cloze2.s: A ___ goal, such as reading twenty pages tonight, is easier to meet than the goal of reading more.

misuse.s: The directions were specific, saying only that the library was somewhere in town.
misuse.why: Specific means exact; saying only 'somewhere in town' is vague.

visual.alt: A map pin placed exactly on a bullseye.

words.def: Using few words to say something clearly.
words.ex: A concise summary can capture a whole chapter in three sentences.
words.ex2: His text message was concise: 'Late. Start without me.'
words.nonExample: A rambling story that never gets to the point is not concise.

apps.academic: A concise conclusion repeats the main claim in one or two sentences.
apps.spoken: Can you give me a concise answer?
apps.writing: Cut repeated words and filler phrases to make a sentence concise.

cloze.s: Because the speaker had only two minutes, she kept her points ___ and clear.

cloze2.s: Write a ___ caption of seven words or fewer that tells the whole story of the photo.

misuse.s: His concise reply filled four pages with long, repeated explanations.
misuse.why: Concise means using few words; four pages of repeated explanations is wordy.

visual.alt: Scissors trimming a long sheet of writing.

words.frame: A concise way to say ___ is ___.

words.def: Using more words than are needed.
words.ex: The verbose speaker took twenty minutes to say what could be said in two.
words.ex2: Her first draft was verbose, with the same idea repeated in three different sentences.
words.nonExample: A short note that says only what is needed is not verbose.

apps.academic: Teachers often mark a verbose sentence and ask the writer to cut it by half.
apps.spoken: Sorry, I'm being verbose; let me get to the point.
apps.writing: To fix a verbose paragraph, circle the ideas you need and delete the rest.

cloze.s: The ___ email repeated the same reminder five times in different words.

cloze2.s: To trim a ___ paragraph, circle the ideas you need and delete everything else.

misuse.s: The verbose author used one short sentence to say everything she meant and wrote nothing more.
misuse.why: Verbose means using more words than needed; one short sentence is the opposite.

visual.alt: A very long scroll beside a speech bubble.

words.frame: A verbose sentence could be shortened by ___.

words.def: Complete and careful, leaving nothing important out.
words.ex: The inspector did a thorough check of every room.
words.ex2: Her thorough notes covered each step of the experiment.
words.nonExample: A quick glance that skips most of the room is not thorough.

apps.academic: A thorough answer addresses every part of the question and cites evidence.
apps.writing: Thorough is easy to confuse with through and though; check the spelling.

cloze.s: After a ___ search of the garage, Dad finally found the missing key behind a paint can.

cloze2.s: The team did a ___ job of cleaning the park, picking up even the smallest pieces of litter.

misuse.s: He did a thorough job by skipping half the steps and leaving the rest unfinished.
misuse.why: Thorough means complete and careful; skipping steps is the opposite.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass beside a completed checklist.

words.frame: A thorough check of ___ would include ___.

words.ex: The intense heat of the desert made the hikers rest every few minutes.
words.ex2: She watched the game with intense focus, never looking away from the ball.
words.nonExample: A gentle breeze is not intense.

apps.academic: Scientists measure the intensity of light, sound, and earthquakes.
apps.writing: Use intense for strong feelings, smells, light, heat, and effort; add a detail to show how.

cloze.s: The ___ light from the welding torch hurt our eyes, so everyone wore dark masks.

cloze2.s: After an ___ week of practice, the band was ready for the concert.

misuse.s: The intense smell was so faint that nobody in the room noticed it at all.
misuse.why: Intense means very strong; a smell that no one notices is faint.

visual.alt: A flame beside a face feeling great heat.

words.frame: The most intense ___ I have felt was ___.

words.def: Not too much and not too little; in the middle.

senses.def: To lead a discussion fairly, or to make something less extreme.
senses.example: The teacher moderated the debate so that every group had a turn.

words.ex: The soup was a moderate temperature, neither cold nor scalding.
words.ex2: Moderate exercise, such as a daily walk, helps keep people healthy.
words.nonExample: A blazing fire is not moderate.
words.rel: in the middle of a scale

apps.academic: A moderate climate has neither extreme heat nor extreme cold.
apps.spoken: I like a moderate amount of spice.
apps.writing: The adjective ends with a short i sound; the verb ends with a long a sound.

cloze.s: The forecast calls for ___ rain, enough to wet the sidewalk but not enough to cancel the game.

cloze2.s: The store's prices were ___: not cheap, but not expensive either.

misuse.s: The moderate storm was the strongest in a hundred years and destroyed the whole town.
misuse.why: Moderate means in the middle; a storm that destroys a town is extreme.

visual.alt: A partly sunny sky above a balanced scale.

words.def: Speaking in a direct way that does not soften hard words.

senses.def: Not sharp; having a dull edge or point.
senses.example: The blunt knife could not cut through the tomato.

words.ex: The doctor was blunt: the cast would stay on for six weeks.
words.ex2: Her blunt feedback stung at first, but it made the essay stronger.
words.nonExample: Hiding a hard truth inside gentle hints is not being blunt.

apps.academic: A blunt statement tells the truth plainly, which can help or hurt depending on tone.
apps.spoken: To be blunt, this plan will not work.
apps.writing: Use blunt for direct speech, and pair it with tactful when you want to soften it.

cloze.s: When Eli asked whether his joke was funny, his sister gave a ___ answer: 'Not really.'

cloze2.s: The coach's ___ advice was that the team should practice twice as much.

misuse.s: She was blunt, using soft hints and gentle words so that her real meaning stayed hidden.
misuse.why: Blunt means direct without softening; soft hints that hide the meaning are not blunt.

visual.alt: A person speaking beside a hammer.

words.def: Gentle or not strong; not harsh or extreme.
words.ex: The curry had a mild flavor, so even young children could eat it.
words.ex2: Winters here are mild, with little snow.
words.nonExample: A blizzard with fierce winds is not mild.

apps.academic: Doctors describe symptoms as mild, moderate, or severe.
apps.writing: Use mild for weather, flavors, and feelings that are gentle, not strong.

cloze.s: Because the winter was ___, the pond never froze solid enough for skating.

cloze2.s: The nurse said the sunburn was ___ and would fade in a day or two.

misuse.s: The mild tornado destroyed every building on the street and flipped over dozens of cars.
misuse.why: Mild means gentle; a tornado that destroys buildings is severe.

visual.alt: A soft cloudy sky with a gently blowing leaf.

words.def: Weak or hard to notice; not clear or strong.

senses.def: To suddenly lose consciousness for a short time.
senses.example: The runner felt dizzy and nearly fainted at the finish line.

words.ex: A faint light glowed from the cabin window far across the lake.
words.ex2: She heard a faint tapping at the door and wondered whether it was the wind.
words.nonExample: A blaring siren is not a faint sound.

apps.academic: Observers recorded a faint star that could not be seen without a telescope.
apps.spoken: I can hear a faint buzzing in the wall.
apps.writing: Use faint for light, sound, smell, or marks that are barely there.

cloze.s: In the dim hall, we could see only a ___ glow from under the door.

cloze2.s: The writing on the old letter was so ___ that she needed a magnifying glass to read it.

misuse.s: The faint sound was so loud that it shook the windows and made everyone cover their ears.
misuse.why: Faint means weak and hard to notice; a sound that shakes windows is loud.

visual.alt: A small candle glowing dimly in the mist.

passage.title: Three Drafts of a Lunch Review
paras: Rin's first draft of her cafeteria review for the school newspaper was short. "The food was okay, and the room was kind of nice," she wrote. Her editor, Ms. Okoye, read it twice and shook her head. "This is vague," she said. "Okay compared to what? Nice how? Give me something specific."

Rin spent the next three days doing thorough research. She ate lunch in the cafeteria every day, took notes on a clipboard, and interviewed six students. Then she wrote a second draft that was four pages long. It described every table, every tray, and the history of the salt shakers. Ms. Okoye smiled politely. "This is verbose," she said. "Your best details are buried. Make it concise."

Rin circled her strongest details and cut the rest. She realized that exact words could do more work than extra words. Instead of writing that the soup smelled strong, she wrote that the onion smell was so intense that it followed you down the hall. The chili had a mild flavor, gentle enough for anyone. The tomato soup was only moderate in heat, neither cold nor steaming. And under every conversation she could hear the faint hum of the dishwashers.

Ms. Okoye's comments on the third draft were blunt but fair. "The first sentence is still weak," she said, "but the rest is exactly what a reader wants." Rin fixed the opening, and the review ran on the front page. That week, three students told her they had tried the chili because of her description. Rin learned that choosing the right word was not about sounding fancy. It was about helping the reader see, smell, and taste what she had noticed.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Ms. Okoye calls the second draft "verbose." This means the draft was
choices: wordy, with more words than needed
qs.why: The draft was four pages long and described every table and the history of the salt shakers, so it used too many words.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Okoye call the first draft vague?
choices: It did not give exact details about the food or the room.
It was written in the wrong order.
It was too long for the newspaper.
It left out the names of the students.
qs.why: Her questions, Okay compared to what? Nice how?, show that the draft lacks specific details.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Rin's research was thorough?
choices: She wrote a second draft that was four pages long.
She ate lunch in the cafeteria every day, took notes, and interviewed six students.
Her review ran on the front page.
qs.why: Thorough means complete and careful, and daily visits, notes, and interviews show that.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the phrase "gentle enough for anyone" helps you understand that the chili's flavor was
qs.why: A flavor that is gentle enough for anyone is not strong, which is what mild means.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Long articles are better than short ones.
Editors should never give honest feedback.
Writers who revise with exact, concise words help readers see and feel what they noticed.
A first draft is usually perfect.
qs.why: Rin revises from vague to verbose to exact and concise, and the final review helps readers experience the cafeteria.

write.prompt: Choose a short sentence you wrote this year that is vague or wordy. Rewrite it so that it is specific and concise, using at least three words from this unit. Then explain which word you changed and why.

study.task: Choose three adjectives from the unit and build the adverb (-ly) and noun (-ness or -ity) from each. Then write one sentence that uses an adverb and one that uses a noun, and explain how the ending changes the part of speech.

When is it better to be blunt, and when is it better to be tactful? Explain.

argue.prompt: Claim: In school writing, a short, concise answer is usually better than a long one. Take a side and support it with two reasons, using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A concise answer can ___, but a thorough answer might ___.

constructed.prompt: Write one vague sentence and one specific sentence about the same event, then explain what makes the second one better.
look: gives two sentences about the same event
names the exact detail that was added
constructed.model: Vague: 'We did something fun after school.' Specific: 'We built a fort from cardboard boxes in Mia's garage.' The second sentence is better because it names exactly what we did and where.

constructed.prompt: Rewrite this verbose sentence so that it is concise: 'Due to the fact that it was raining outside, we made the decision to stay inside the house.' Explain what you cut.
look: produces a shorter sentence with the same meaning
names the filler words that were removed
constructed.model: Concise: 'Because it was raining, we stayed home.' The original was verbose because 'Due to the fact that' and 'made the decision to' added words without adding meaning.

constructed.prompt: Describe a thunderstorm in four sentences, using faint, mild, moderate, and intense to show it growing stronger.
look: places the words in increasing order of strength
adds a concrete detail to each
constructed.model: At first the thunder was a faint rumble. Soon a mild rain tapped the roof, and then the wind grew moderate and bent the trees. By midnight the lightning was so intense that the whole yard flashed white.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten adjectives for choosing the exact word, organized as ladders of strength (faint, mild, moderate, intense), pairs of precision and length (vague/specific, concise/verbose), and two words for style (thorough, blunt). They read a narrative about three drafts of a review, practice revising, and write about their own sentences.

notes.va.vague.adj: Vague is missing exact detail. Use a quick revision routine: circle a vague word, ask who, what, where, when, and replace it. Students often assume vague means untrue; it only means not exact.
notes.va.specific.adj: Specific is the opposite of vague. Teach a specific noun and verb swap: went becomes sprinted, thing becomes backpack. Connect to text evidence: a specific detail beats a general claim.
notes.va.concise.adj: Concise is few words, clear meaning. It is not the same as short; a short vague sentence is not concise. Practice cutting filler such as due to the fact that.
notes.va.verbose.adj: Verbose is too many words. Use a sentence from a student draft (with permission) and cut it together. Avoid shaming; the goal is a better sentence.
notes.va.thorough.adj: Thorough is complete and careful. It is a confusable spelling: thorough, through, though. Say each aloud and write a sentence for each. Ask what a thorough check of a science lab looks like.
notes.va.intense.adj: Intense is very strong. Place on a ladder with faint, mild, and moderate. Students sometimes use intense as a filler for any strong feeling; ask for the detail that proves it.
notes.va.moderate.adj: Moderate is in the middle. Teach the adjective first and name the verb sense (to lead a discussion or make less extreme). Pronunciation changes with part of speech. Use weather and spice examples.
notes.va.blunt.adj: Blunt is direct without softening. Name the other sense (not sharp). Connect to candid and tactful from unit 1: blunt is more direct than candid. Role-play a blunt and a tactful version of the same advice.
notes.va.mild.adj: Mild is gentle or not strong. Use medical language (mild, moderate, severe) and weather. Contrast with intense on the ladder.
notes.va.faint.adj: Faint is barely noticeable. Name the second sense (to pass out) so students do not become confused. Contrast with invisible and inaudible from the previous unit: faint can still be seen or heard.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The sentence says the soup smelled strong. Strong is a little vague. The passage says the onion smell was intense and followed you down the hall. Intense is stronger than mild or moderate, and the detail about the hall proves it. I can choose the word by asking how strong the thing is.'
discuss: Which word on the strength ladder is hardest to place, and why?
How do you know when a sentence is concise and when it is too short to be clear?
misconceptions: Concise means as short as possible.
Mild and faint mean the same thing.
extend: Rewrite a paragraph from a draft by replacing every vague word with a specific one and cutting at least three filler phrases.
Make a four-step ladder for another quality (for example, temperature or size) and write a sentence for each rung.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the strength ladder two days later with a card sort and at one week by having students revise a short paragraph. Connect to subtle, candid, reiterate, and logical from earlier units as other words that fine-tune meaning.

frames: A faint ___ is ___, but an intense ___ is ___.
My first sentence was vague because ___. A specific version is ___.
To be concise, I can cut ___ and keep ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads a vague sentence aloud. Partner B asks one question (who, what, where, or when) to make it specific, then restates it in fewer words.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: vago, específico, conciso, verboso, minucioso, intenso, moderado, directo (blunt; franco and brusco are options), suave (mild), tenue (faint).
Sense boundaries: moderate (verb sense in senses), blunt (not-sharp sense in senses), faint (to pass out in senses); thorough taught as a confusable spelling.

The strength ladder faint, mild, moderate, intense is a teaching simplification: intense and faint also apply to different kinds of qualities (feeling, light, sound) and not every word fits every noun.
Passage is fiction about a student newspaper review; no real school is described.
